title: Ignatius of Antioch
lead: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, was taken under guard to Rome to die by wild beasts; Jerome says he 'was put to death the eleventh year of Trajan' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). He opens his letter to Polycarp as 'Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus'. On the way he wrote seven letters to churches of Asia, to Rome and to Polycarp. They are in no church's Bible. The works list calls them the Letters of Ignatius. All seven are translated on this site, each as its own book.

sections.b: Eusebius says Ignatius was 'chosen bishop of Antioch, second in succession to Peter', was 'sent from Syria to Rome' and 'became food for wild beasts on account of his testimony to Christ'. He wrote from Smyrna to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians and Romans, and from Troas to the Philadelphians, the Smyrnaeans and Polycarp (Church History 3.36.2-10, NPNF). Polycarp sent copies of the letters he had to the Philippians (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2), whose wish 'to make a collection of the letters of Ignatius', Lake says, called his own letter forth.

sections.h: The seven letters on the site
sections.b:
The site translates all seven letters from Lake's Greek of the short recension. Ignatius to the Ephesians, written from Smyrna, thanks the church that sent its overseer Onesimus to meet him and sets out the letters' great themes: unity with the overseer, Christ 'God in man', and the one bread, 'the medicine of immortality'. Ignatius to the Romans, also from Smyrna, asks the Roman Christians not to save him from the beasts: 'I am God's wheat'. Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, from Troas, argues against those who said Christ suffered only in appearance, and has 'the catholic church' (8:2), which the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) and a district calendar of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod call the first use of the phrase.

From Smyrna Ignatius also wrote to Magnesia and Tralles, whose overseers Damas and Polybius had come to him (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.5). Ignatius to the Magnesians sets the overseer 'in the place of God' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1), warns against living 'by Judaism', and holds the much-quoted 'no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day]' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1) and the earliest known uses of the word 'Christianity' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:3, as Lightfoot says). Ignatius to the Trallians says of overseer, elders and deacons, 'Without these, it is not called a church' (Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1), and answers those who said Christ suffered 'only in appearance' with a confession built on 'truly' (Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2).

From Troas, Ignatius wrote back to Philadelphia, a church he had visited on the road: Ignatius to the Philadelphians calls it to 'one thanksgiving', 'one altar' and 'one overseer' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 4:1) and answers those who would believe nothing they could not find 'in the archives': 'to me Jesus Christ is the archives' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2). Ignatius to Polycarp, to the overseer of Smyrna, is the only one of the seven letters addressed to one person: short rules for a church leader, and a request to choose a messenger for Syria, because his sudden sailing from Troas to Neapolis kept him from writing to all the churches (Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2-8:1).
